opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it was quite an experience. We started out with a fairly small prototype, just trying to see whether the core idea worked at all: a model that, instead of getting deeper by adding more layers, reuses a recurrent block in latent space. At test time you can iterate that block more times and spend more compute thinking about a problem, without producing more tokens. At small scale it looked promising, but you never really know whether something like that survives scaling until you try it.

Moving to Frontier was a big jump. Frontier is an AMD machine, so a lot of the usual tooling people take for granted on NVIDIA clusters either didn't exist or didn't work out of the box. We spent a significant amount of time on the engineering side: getting the software stack to run reliably, making communication efficient across that many nodes, and dealing with hardware and node failures, which at 4,000 GPUs simply happen regularly. A good part of the project was just making the training robust enough to keep going.

The more interesting surprise was on the modeling side. Recurrent-depth models are a lot less forgiving than standard transformers. Our first large runs failed in ways we hadn't seen at small scale. In one run the model basically learned to ignore the recurrence: the hidden state collapsed, and the model stopped using the extra iterations in any meaningful way. So it trained, but it didn't do the thing we wanted. In another run we had stability problems. We had to go back and rethink details like normalization placement, how the input is injected into each recurrent step, initialization, and how we sample the number of recurrent iterations during training, so the model actually learns to use variable compute.

Only after those fixes did we get a run that behaved the way we hoped, where more iterations at test time actually translated into better performance, especially on reasoning-heavy tasks like math and code. So my takeaway is that small-scale prototypes are necessary but not sufficient. Some of the most important lessons only show up at scale, and with a novel architecture you should budget for a few failed runs before getting a good one.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was a fun one. The honest answer is that we didn't start out planning to go to 4,000 GPUs. The project started as a pretty small research question: can you get a transformer to do more "thinking" by looping a block of layers in latent space, rather than by generating more tokens? So the first prototypes were tiny, trained on a handful of GPUs, just to see whether the recurrence did anything interesting at all.

The jump to Frontier came through a collaboration with Oak Ridge, and Frontier is a very particular machine. It's AMD hardware, so MI250X GPUs, and the software stack is not the stack most of us in the language modeling world are used to. A lot of the standard tooling for large-scale pretraining assumes NVIDIA, assumes a certain kind of interconnect, assumes certain fused kernels exist. On Frontier, a lot of that just wasn't there, or it was there in a half-working form. So a surprising amount of the effort went into things that have nothing to do with the research idea: getting the compilation to be stable, getting the communication collectives to not fall over, figuring out why one node out of hundreds was slow and dragging everything else down.

And the way scheduling works on a machine like that shapes the whole experience. You don't get the system continuously. You get allocations, big ones, for a window of time, and then you're done. So you can't iterate the way you would on a cluster you own. You have to be very deliberate: everything gets tested at small scale, then medium scale, and by the time you're on the full allocation, you really want the run to just go. We still had surprises. Things that worked at 500 GPUs behaved differently at 4,000, mostly around the networking and the occasional hardware fault. You learn to build in checkpointing and restarts as a first-class part of the training loop rather than as an afterthought.

The other thing that was interesting from a research perspective is that the recurrent architecture interacts with scaling in ways a standard transformer doesn't. Because we sample a random number of recurrence steps during training, the compute per batch varies, and that has consequences for throughput, for the optimizer, for how you think about what a "token budget" even means. There were moments in the run where the loss did things we hadn't seen at small scale, and we had to decide, in real time with a limited allocation, whether that was a bug, an instability, or just the model doing something we didn't understand yet. Some of those we resolved, some we just lived with and documented.

But I'd say the experience overall was a reminder that the research idea is maybe twenty percent of the work. The other eighty is engineering, logistics, and a fair amount of patience. And I think it's actually valuable that an academic group did this, because it shows that you can take a somewhat unconventional architecture to real scale without a frontier-lab budget, provided you have access to the compute and you're willing to deal with the rough edges.

astra-6.text:
It was a big jump. With a small prototype, you can focus on the idea: does recurrence work, and does the model learn? At the scale of 4,000 GPUs, you also have to ask whether you can run that experiment efficiently and reliably. The model and the infrastructure become much harder to separate.

With recurrence, you’re repeatedly applying computation to a hidden state, so the amount of computation you do is itself an important part of the experiment. That makes the transition interesting: you’re trying to preserve the flexibility that motivated the architecture while making it practical at scale.

I’d hesitate to give a detailed account of particular failures or breakthroughs without those details in front of me, but that’s the central tension—taking something that’s compelling as a research idea and making it work as a large training run.

sol-6.1.text:
The interesting thing is that you’re scaling two things at once: the model and the system that lets you experiment with it. With a small prototype, you can change an idea, run it, and get feedback quickly. At 4,000 GPUs, getting that feedback becomes a substantial engineering problem in its own right.

For a recurrent model, there’s also this distinction between making the model larger and giving it more computation by repeating the recurrent block. So you have to think carefully about what you’re scaling and whether the additional computation is actually helping.

The challenge is keeping that scientific question visible while you’re dealing with distributed training. Getting a run to execute at that scale is one milestone; getting a run that tells you something useful about the architecture is the real goal.
